title: Associations Among Daily Screen Time, Digital Addiction, Sleep Quality, and Digital Eye Strain in University Students: A Structural Equation Modeling Study
content: Background/Objectives: The widespread use of digital technologies has raised con-cerns regarding the health consequences of prolonged screen exposure, particularly among university students. Although previous studies have separately examined digi-tal addiction, sleep quality, and digital eye strain, the interrelationships among these factors remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate the associa-tions among daily screen time, digital addiction, sleep quality, and digital eye strain using a structural equation modeling approach. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 410 university students enrolled in a Faculty of Health Sciences. Data were collected using the Digital Addiction Scale (DAS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Digital Eye Strain Questionnaire (DESQ). Pearson correlation analysis, multiple linear regression analysis with HC3 robust standard errors, and structural equation modeling with 5000 bootstrap resamples were performed. Results: Higher daily screen time was significantly associated with increased digital addiction (β = 0.582, p < 0.001), poorer sleep quality (β = 0.441, p < 0.001), and greater digital eye strain (β = 0.684, p < 0.001). Digital addiction (β = 0.338, p < 0.001) and poor sleep qua-lity (β = 0.281, p < 0.001) were also significantly associated with digital eye strain. The structural model demonstrated good fit indices (χ²/df = 1.96, CFI = 0.962, TLI = 0.951, RMSEA = 0.047, and SRMR = 0.041). Bootstrap analyses revealed significant indirect associations of digital addiction and sleep quality in the relationship between screen time and digital eye strain. Conclusions: Higher daily screen time was associated with greater digital eye strain among university students. Digital addiction and poor sleep quality may represent important explanatory factors linking screen exposure to visual symptoms. These findings suggest that interventions promoting healthy digital beha-viors and sleep hygiene may contribute to reducing screen-related ocular symptoms in young adults. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationships among these variables.
